name: Facial analysis YouTube channels

lead: Facial analysis channels are creators who break down and rate faces, often using community scales like PSL. They are part of looksmaxxing's online culture.
The ratings are not scientifically validated, and critics call parts of the scale pseudoscientific.

paras: Creators assess features such as eye tilt, jawline and cheeks, then assign a tier or score and suggest changes, from skincare to surgery.
Press coverage has linked appearance-rating communities with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation. No studies have examined the content itself.

lead: Facial analysis content is video and livestream material in which creators assess faces, rating features such as eye shape, jawline and cheeks, often against community scales like the PSL scale. It is a staple of looksmaxxing culture online.[1]

Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing describes the practice as spreading from incel-era forums to TikTok in the 2020s and names livestreamers such as Clavicular and Androgenic; it does not discuss YouTube channels specifically.[1] Critics describe PSL-style ratings as pseudoscientific, and press coverage has linked appearance-rating communities to body dysmorphia.[1]
No studies have examined facial analysis channels or their viewers.

paras: Content in this category assesses features believed to affect attractiveness, such as positive canthal tilt ('hunter eyes'), hollow cheeks and a defined jawline, and often places faces on a tier scale. Sources disagree on the tiers; one overview lists seven, from 'subhuman' to 'giga Chad', while another lists three.[1]

The term looksmaxxing was coined on incel message boards in the 2010s, and early culture was shaped by forums such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, now defunct.[1] The trend was popularized on TikTok in the 2020s and covered by outlets including the New York Times and Business Insider in November 2023.[1]

Commentators and researchers describe the practice as judgmental and reliant on anecdote.[1] Reports in outlets including the BBC and Guardian have linked communities that rate appearance with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, and one researcher argues algorithms can draw young men toward incel views.[1]
